hypotheses.hypothesis: Addition of a small amount of chromium (≈5 at%) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby improving oxygen resistance without compromising the alloy’s mechanical performance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single-phase or near-homogeneous microstructure providing 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce ≈5 at% chromium to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr formulation while keeping the remaining elemental ratios nearly unchanged.
hypotheses.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for durations up to 200 hours; mechanical properties evaluated at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer formed at the alloy surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: The added Cr reacts preferentially with the already present Ta during oxidation to form a CrTaO4-based layer. At elevated temperatures (≈1100 °C), enhanced diffusion kinetics facilitate the formation of a more uniform and less porous CrTaO4 scale, which in turn impedes the inward transport of oxygen. This protective scale mimics the beneficial effect observed in the NV1 alloy, where denser CrTaO4 formation at higher temperatures resulted in lower mass gains (PMC6513993::web::009, PMC6513993::web::011).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation mass gain (expected to be in the lower range of ~4 mg/cm² or less after 200 hours at 1100 °C) relative to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, with preservation of room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance with mass gains that would compromise long-term high-temperature applications.
hypotheses.boundary: Intervention must maintain the alloy’s microstructure so that the ductility (8–16% RT tensile ductility) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) are not significantly degraded.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact optimal Cr content and its impact on phase stability in the equiatomic alloy need careful optimization; quantitative reduction in mass gain is estimated by analogy to NV1 but precise values for HfNbTaTiZr are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast alloys: one equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one with ≈5 at% Cr addition (adjusting other element proportions slightly so that the overall alloy remains refractory). Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for 200 hours. Then, measure mass gain per unit area and examine the oxide scale by XRD and SEM/EDS.
measurements: Mass gain (mg/cm²) vs. time
Phase identification of oxide scale (XRD)
Microstructural analysis of oxide layer density and continuity (SEM/EDS)
Retention of mechanical properties via tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-added alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain (or if the oxide scale remains porous and discontinuous) relative to the untreated alloy, or if key mechanical properties are degraded, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that formation of a denser CrTaO4-based oxide layer at elevated temperatures (1100 °C) contributes to improved oxidation resistance in the NV1 alloy (PMC6513993::web::009, PMC6513993::web::011)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis transfers the oxidation-protective mechanism (CrTaO4 formation) to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr system by a targeted Cr addition, rather than relying on the complex multi-element design used in NV1.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor addition of yttrium (≈0.3–0.5 at%) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve the adhesion and integrity of any oxide scale formed during high-temperature oxidation, thereby further enhancing oxygen resistance while maintaining mechanical performance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr characterized by its high tensile ductility and yield strength at high temperatures, but with an oxide scale that is prone to spallation or porosity under prolonged oxidation.
hypotheses.intervention: Doping the alloy with a trace amount (≈0.3–0.5 at%) of yttrium, with all other elements kept at their equiatomic ratios.
hypotheses.conditions: Oxidation test in flowing dry air at 1000–1100 °C for up to 200 hours, and subsequent mechanical evaluations at room temperature and high temperature (≈1000 °C) under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced oxide scale adhesion and reduced porosity/spallation in the externally formed oxide layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: Yttrium is a well-known reactive element used in superalloys (as noted in teaching texts on superalloy development) to improve oxide-scale adherence. In this context, Y is expected to segregate to the grain boundaries of the nascent oxide layer (which may be based on CrTaO4 or mixed oxides), reducing interfacial stresses and inhibiting the formation of cracks or pores. This modification is anticipated to retard further oxygen ingress, similar to the beneficial effects observed in other high-temperature alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002, TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::012).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A lower overall oxidation mass gain compared to undoped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, with the oxide scale showing improved continuity and adhesion along with minimal spallation, while mechanical properties remain essentially unaltered.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated equiatomic alloy shows inadequate oxygen resistance partly due to the formation of porous or spalling oxide layers during long-term oxidation.
hypotheses.boundary: The addition of yttrium must remain low enough (≈0.3–0.5 at%) to avoid formation of separate Y-rich phases that could impair the alloy’s ductility or strength.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the beneficial role of Y in oxide scale adhesion is well established in superalloys, its exact effect in refractory equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, with its distinct high-temperature oxidation mechanisms, is less certain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr: one without yttrium and one containing ≈0.3–0.5 at% Y. Subject both to oxidation in flowing air at 1000–1100 °C for 200 hours and conduct post-exposure analysis of oxide scale morphology (via SEM/EDS) and mass gain measurement. Perform mechanical tests to check retention of ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Mass gain vs. time
SEM/EDS mapping of oxide scale for adherence and porosity
XRD phase analysis of the oxide film
Mechanical tensile tests at room and high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Y-doped samples do not show improved oxide scale integrity (reduced porosity/spallation) and lower mass gain compared to undoped samples, or if there is degradation of mechanical performance, the hypothesis is refuted.

hypotheses.builds_on: the general principle from superalloy technology of using reactive element additions (like Y) to stabilize and adhere protective oxide scales, extended here to a refractory equiatomic system.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a single reactive-element intervention (yttrium addition) applied to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to improve the quality and stability of the oxide scale, a strategy not explored in the referenced paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introducing a minor silicon addition (≈2–3 at%) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will induce the formation of a denser, possibly mixed (Cr,Si)-based oxide scale that offers improved oxygen barrier properties while preserving the alloy's mechanical performance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting high-temperature strength and ductility but prone to forming nonuniform or porous oxide layers during prolonged oxygen exposure.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding ≈2–3 at% Si to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, keeping the balance of elements nearly equiatomic.
hypotheses.conditions: Examine oxidation behavior in flowing air at 1100 °C for durations up to 200 hours, with mechanical performance assessed at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A continuous, less porous mixed oxide scale that incorporates silicon, which may promote the formation of a (Cr,Si)-rich oxide or assist in stabilizing the existing CrTaO4-based layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: The introduction of silicon is expected to modify the oxidation pathway by enabling the formation of a mixed oxide (potentially a (Cr,Si)-rich scale) that is denser and has lower oxygen permeability. In the NV1 alloy discussed in the paper, Si was found to segregate to certain regions and influence oxidation/nitridation behavior (PMC6513993::web::005, PMC6513993::web::014). Here, Si could react with available Cr or Ta oxides to reinforce the barrier effect, thereby reducing further inward oxygen transport while minimally affecting the microstructure and mechanical behavior.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A reduced oxidation mass gain (targeting values similar to or lower than ~4 mg/cm² after 200 hours at 1100 °C) with an oxide layer that exhibits improved density and continuity. The mechanical properties should remain within the design constraints, preserving the ductility and high-temperature strength.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance due to the formation of porous and inhomogeneous oxide scales.
hypotheses.boundary: Si addition must be controlled (≈2–3 at%) to avoid the formation of brittle silicide phases or excessive changes in the alloy’s overall phase stability that could compromise ductility.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise nature and protective efficacy of the mixed (Cr,Si)-based oxide in this system are less well established; quantitative improvements in oxygen resistance need experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys with and without 2–3 at% Si. Subject both compositions to isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for 200 hours. Characterize the oxide scale (using SEM/EDS, XRD) and measure the mass gain. Carry out mechanical tests to ensure that ductility and yield strength are maintained.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain measurements
XRD and SEM/EDS analysis of the scale for phase and density
Mechanical property tests (tensile testing) at room and high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-doped alloy does not exhibit a denser, lower-permeability oxide scale with a measurable reduction in mass gain compared to the undoped alloy, or if there is a significant adverse effect on mechanical performance, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation that Si addition in NV1 influenced the oxidation/nitridation pattern, suggesting its role in modifying oxide scale formation (PMC6513993::web::005, PMC6513993::web::014)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the role of Si beyond nitridation resistance to actively modifying and densifying the oxide scale on a refractory equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, a strategy not addressed in the reported work.

paper_did: Prepared and characterized a novel refractory high‐entropy alloy (NV1) with composition including Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, and Ti, featuring a dendritic microstructure with Mo‐rich, Cr‐rich, and Al‐rich regions.

Conducted long‐term isothermal oxidation tests at 1000 °C and 1100 °C (up to 200 hours) using thermogravimetric analysis and muffle furnace experiments, with detailed pre‐ and post- oxidation microstructural, phase (XRD) and chemical (EDS, TEM) analyses.

Analyzed oxidation kinetics and mechanisms, demonstrating that at 1000 °C the porous CrTaO4-based oxide led to an exponential mass gain (6.53 mg/cm²) while at 1100 °C the formation of a denser CrTaO4-based oxide (with accompanying parabolic kinetics) reduced mass gain to 4.03 mg/cm².
paper_reported: The NV1 alloy forms predominantly CrTaO4-based oxide scales with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3 during high-temperature oxidation.

At 1000 °C, inadequate diffusion kinetics result in a porous, continuously thickening oxide scale and significant overall mass gain, while at 1100 °C a denser and more protective oxide layer forms, leading to lower net oxidation.
Oxidation and nitridation phenomena (e.g., formation of TiN and internal Al2O3 dispersion) were observed and linked to local chemical heterogeneities and diffusion limitations.
paper_proposed: Further investigation of the nature and stability of the CrTaO4-based oxide, including its non-stoichiometric composition and lattice variations with temperature.
Clarification of the roles of internal oxidation and nitridation (and the influence of elements like Si) in long-term high-temperature exposures.
Exploration of alloy design strategies (e.g., optimized elemental additions) to enhance oxidation and nitridation resistance in RHEAs over prolonged service durations.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Partial Substitution of Hf with Additional Cr to Enable Dense Cr‐Based Protective Oxide Formation
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which in its as-cast state shows 8–16% room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance due to unprotective oxide scales.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by substituting approximately 10 at% of Hf with Cr. This raises the overall Cr content (from 0 to about 10 at%) while slightly reducing Hf, aiming to promote formation of a robust Cr-containing oxide scale.
hypotheses.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for durations up to 200 hours; tensile and yield properties evaluated at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense oxide scale that is rich in Cr (likely in a Cr–Ta–O formulation) and that suppresses oxygen ingress.
hypotheses.mechanism: Thermodynamic and kinetic considerations indicate that increased Cr content can drive the formation of a protective oxide by reacting preferentially with available Ta and potentially other oxide‐forming elements. In alloys similar to NV1, a sufficiently high Cr level enabled a denser, less porous Cr-based oxide (e.g. CrTaO₄-like) when oxidation kinetics are favorable at 1100 °C. Here, by raising Cr (via partial Hf substitution), the oxidation pathway is shifted to favor formation of a continuous protective scale that can outcompete the formation of less protective HfO₂ or ZrO₂.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Reduction in oxidation mass gain (targeting levels near or below ~4 mg/cm² after 200 hours at 1100 °C) with a dense and adherent Cr-containing oxide scale and preservation of the alloy’s mechanical properties.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which forms less protective, porous oxides under similar oxidation conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: The Cr substitution level must remain low enough (~10 at%) so that key mechanical properties (ductility, yield strength) are not compromised by formation of brittle intermetallics or drastic microstructural changes.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While model systems (e.g. NV1) suggest benefits from higher Cr content, the precise reaction pathways in a HfNbTaTiZr system and the competition with HfO₂/ZrO₂ formation require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys: one standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a modified alloy where ~10 at% of Hf is replaced by Cr. Expose both to isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for 200 hours. Post-test, record the mass gain per unit area, perform XRD to detect oxide phases, and use SEM/EDS to assess oxide scale density and continuity. Also, conduct tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain vs. time
Phase identification via XRD and microstructural analysis via SEM/EDS
Tensile ductility and yield strength measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain (or if the oxide scale remains porous/discontinuous) relative to the control, or if mechanical performance is degraded beyond acceptable limits, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that a dense CrTaO₄-based oxide layer formed at 1100 °C improved oxidation resistance in NV1, but recognizes that the beneficial effect in NV1 is tied to a sufficiently high Cr content.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis adapts the protective mechanism observed in NV1 by deliberately altering the composition of HfNbTaTiZr (which originally lacks Cr) to promote in situ formation of a more protective Cr-containing oxide scale.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Pre‐Oxidation Surface Treatment to Form an In Situ Protective Oxide Nanolayer
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that shows acceptable mechanical properties but develops nonuniform and porous oxide scales when exposed directly to high-temperature oxidation conditions.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the as-cast alloy to a controlled short-duration pre-oxidation treatment in a mildly oxidizing (or low oxygen partial pressure) atmosphere at an intermediate temperature (e.g., ~900 °C for 1–2 hours) prior to service exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: After pre-oxidation, expose the samples to isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours; evaluate mechanical properties at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous, and adherent oxide nanolayer that acts as a diffusion barrier, limiting further inward oxygen transport during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.mechanism: Controlled pre-oxidation allows formation of an ultrathin, uniform oxide film (potentially containing a mix of native oxides from Nb, Ta, Ti, Hf, and Zr) without the evolution of defects typical of long-term uncontrolled oxidation. This pre-formed scale can heal or coalesce during subsequent high-temperature exposure, serving as a barrier much like the dense CrTaO₄ layer observed in NV1 at higher temperatures. The concept is analogous to pre-oxidation treatments used in some superalloys to improve scale adherence and protect against rapid oxidation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized alloy is expected to show significantly lower oxidation mass gain during the 200-hour exposure at 1100 °C, as evidenced by a more uniform and less porous oxide scale, while retaining the prescribed room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated equiatomic alloy exhibits excessive oxidation due to the formation of porous or discontinuous scales during direct exposure at high temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: The pre-oxidation treatment parameters (temperature, time, oxygen partial pressure) must be optimized so as to form a protective scale without inducing deleterious phase changes or surface embrittlement that could lower ductility.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact composition, thickness, and long-term stability of the pre-formed oxide nanolayer in a HfNbTaTiZr matrix are not well established; the quantitative benefit relative to direct high-temperature oxidation awaits experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one receiving the pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., 900 °C in a controlled low-oxygen atmosphere for 1–2 hours) and one untreated. Subsequently, subject both groups to isothermal oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for 200 hours. Evaluate oxidation mass gain, analyze the oxide layer’s morphology (using SEM/EDS and XRD), and perform tensile tests to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain vs. time
Oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and composition via SEM/EDS and XRD
Room-temperature and 1000 °C tensile properties
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-oxidized samples do not show a measurable reduction in oxidation mass gain or exhibit degraded mechanical properties compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the insight that a continuous, dense oxide layer (as observed in NV1 at 1100 °C) can protect against oxidation by limiting oxygen ingress. This treatment seeks to form a similar protective barrier in the HfNbTaTiZr system through processing rather than compositional change.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Instead of altering composition, this hypothesis proposes a novel processing route—controlled pre-oxidation—to deliberately engineer a protective oxide nanolayer on an alloy that otherwise develops inadequate and porous oxide scales.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor Aluminum Addition to Enable Formation of a Protective Alumina Scale
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which currently lacks elements like Al and thus does not develop the highly protective alumina (Al₂O₃) scale known from superalloys.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a small amount of aluminum (~3–5 at%) to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr while adjusting the other elemental proportions slightly to maintain a near-equiatomic balance.
hypotheses.conditions: Perform isothermal oxidation tests in flowing air at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours; subsequently assess mechanical properties at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: An externally formed, continuous, and adherent Al₂O₃ scale that offers excellent oxygen barrier properties.
hypotheses.mechanism: Thermodynamically, alumina is one of the most stable oxides at high temperatures and exhibits extremely low oxygen permeability. By introducing a modest level of Al, the alloy is enabled to form a thin, coherent Al₂O₃ layer during initial oxidation stages. Although the kinetics of alumina formation can be challenging in complex refractory alloys, careful design of the Al content (low enough to avoid brittle phase formation) may activate a self-healing protective behavior similar to that used in Ni-based superalloys. The formation of Al₂O₃ can hinder oxygen transport and thus improve oxidation resistance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation mass gain (targeting values around or below ~4 mg/cm² after 200 hours at 1100 °C) should be observed, alongside the formation of a uniform alumina scale that preserves the alloy’s mechanical performance.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr forms nonprotective, porous oxide scales that permit rapid oxygen ingress during extended high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.boundary: The Al addition must be limited (~3–5 at%) to avoid formation of brittle intermetallic phases and ensure that the alloy’s ductility and high-temperature strength remain within acceptable ranges.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While protective alumina scales have been well documented in other high-temperature alloys, the exact kinetics of Al₂O₃ formation in a HfNbTaTiZr matrix (with its complex high-melting constituents) are not fully predictable without experimental study.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of alloys: one set with the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another with an addition of ~3–5 at% Al (with slight adjustments to maintain near-equiatomic ratios). Subject both to oxidation in flowing air at 1100 °C for 200 hours. Characterize the oxide scale using XRD and SEM/EDS, measure oxidation mass gain, and conduct mechanical tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain vs. time
Phase and microstructural analysis of the surface oxide via XRD and SEM/EDS
Tensile and yield strength measurements at specified temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not form a continuous, protective alumina scale leading to a significant reduction in oxidation mass gain, or if mechanical properties are adversely affected, then the hypothesis is refuted.

hypotheses.builds_on: the widely recognized principle in superalloy technology that even minor aluminum additions can lead to the formation of a highly protective α-Al₂O₃ scale, a mechanism that has not been previously applied to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a targeted aluminum addition into an otherwise Al-free equiatomic refractory alloy to trigger a protective oxidation mechanism known for its effectiveness in high-temperature superalloys, thereby offering a potentially transformative route to enhance oxygen resistance.

paper_did: Tested a novel refractory high‐entropy alloy (NV1) with composition based on Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, and Ti.
Conducted long‐term isothermal oxidation experiments in flowing dry air at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for durations up to 200 hours, using thermogravimetric analysis and muffle‐furnace treatments.

Characterized the as‐cast and oxidized microstructures and phase evolutions via XRD, SEM with EDS, EPMA, and TEM to examine the formation of external oxide layers, internal oxidation, and nitridation phenomena.
paper_reported: At 1000 °C, NV1 exhibited an exponential oxidation mass gain (~6.53 mg/cm² after 200 hours) due to the development of a porous, CrTaO₄‐based oxide interspersed with dispersed Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃, along with evidence of internal oxidation and TiN nitridation.

At 1100 °C, the oxidation behavior divided into three distinct stages with a lower overall mass gain (~4.03 mg/cm² after 200 hours), attributed to enhanced diffusion kinetics that promoted the formation of a denser, more continuous CrTaO₄‐based oxide layer acting as a partial barrier.

The microstructural analyses revealed phase‐dependent oxidation (with Mo-rich dendrites and Cr- and Al-rich interdendritic regions) and highlighted that the nature (non‐stoichiometric composition) and defect content of the protective CrTaO₄-based oxide controlled oxidation resistance.
paper_proposed: Future work to more carefully examine the nature, non-stoichiometric composition, and protective mechanism of the CrTaO₄-based external oxide.
Investigations into the effects of minor alloying additions (e.g., Si) and the role of nitridation on long-term oxidation behavior to further improve oxidation and nitridation resistance.
Extended studies (beyond the common 48-hour tests) to understand the interplay between external oxidation, internal oxidation, and nitridation over prolonged exposures.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide diffusion coating to the surface of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures while preserving its inherent mechanical properties.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Cast, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with known ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength as reported, but suffering from inadequate oxidation resistance in air.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform a surface pack-aluminizing treatment followed by a brief diffusion heat treatment to develop a thin (few microns) aluminide layer that can transform into an adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 scale during service.
hypotheses.conditions: Post-coating, the alloy is exposed to air at 800–1000 °C for up to 5 hours; mechanical tests (tensile and compression) should be carried out at room temperature and elevated temperatures under strain rates similar to 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that forms on the surface during high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.mechanism: The aluminide coating supplies internal aluminum that diffuses outward at service temperatures, reacting with oxygen to form a protective Al2O3 layer. This oxide is slow growing, chemically stable, and acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress, thereby suppressing pesting without affecting the bulk’s solid solution microstructure and mechanical performance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation (lower weight gain and oxide scale thickness) at 800–1000 °C compared with untreated samples, with negligible degradation in room- and high-temperature ductility and strength (expected retention within the original performance bands).
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows rapid oxidation and pesting in air at elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: The coating must be thin and well-adhered such that the aluminide processing does not excessively alter the near-surface composition or induce residual stresses; intended for temperatures between 800 and 1000 °C and exposure times up to 5 h.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact diffusion kinetics and scale adhesion on this specific RHEA are not fully established; the size of improvement in oxidation resistance is estimated qualitatively rather than quantitatively.

paper_did: Fabricated a series of refractory high‐entropy alloys using the subtraction method (starting from equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and then removing one element at a time) via vacuum‐arc melting, with repeated re‐melting for chemical homogeneity.
Characterized the microstructure and phase formation using X‐ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy (with EDS), confirming a single BCC disordered solid solution in all alloys.

Measured mechanical properties through compression tests at room and elevated temperatures (up to 1400 °C) and analyzed the contribution of each element to yield strength, ductility, and work hardening behavior.

Calculated the solution strengthening effect using established models based on atomic size and shear modulus mismatches, noting that the effective shear modulus is ~30% lower than predicted due to severe lattice distortion.
paper_reported: All the investigated alloys (including HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi) form a single BCC disordered solid solution phase without any observed intermetallics or Laves phases.

Variations in mechanical performance were reported; for instance, the addition of Mo markedly increased room‐temperature yield strength while the removal of Nb enhanced ductility, and alloys with higher melting‐point elements performed better at elevated temperatures.

HfMoNbTaTi was identified as having the best overall performance (27% compressive strain at room temperature and good yield strength at high temperature), and the trends were linked to the elemental solid solution strengthening effects.
paper_proposed: The paper proposed that further refinement of composition (for example, adjusting the amounts of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr) could tailor the alloy properties, and that additional modifications such as the use of anti‐oxidation coatings might be necessary to enable high‐temperature applications in air.
It suggested that more Nb might be added for improved ductility and that the overall insights from the elemental effects could be extended to other RHEA systems, albeit with further research needed.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produced by casting with no deliberate oxide‐forming elements.
hypotheses.intervention: Substitute approximately 5 atomic percent of one of the original refractory elements with Al to yield an alloy composition such as HfNb(Ta-5 at.%)TiZr + 5 at.%Al.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposure in air at high temperatures between 800 °C and 1200 °C for durations up to 5 hours; standard tensile and yield tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous and self-healing alumina (α-Al2O3) scale on the surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: At high temperatures, the additional Al preferentially oxidizes to form an external alumina scale. Due to the low oxygen diffusivity and slow growth kinetics of alumina, the scale acts as a barrier against further oxygen ingress. Similar principles were exploited in alumina-forming alloys reported in PMC6427440 (sections 1 and 2) and align with oxidation protection concepts in high-temperature alloys (KG::al2o3::8ee5dcc665).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation rate and pesting, with retention of the baseline mechanical properties (yield strength ~163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and room-temperature ductility of 8–16%), though the precise improvement magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with inadequate oxygen resistance in air at high temperature.
hypotheses.boundary: Test temperatures between 800 °C and 1200 °C; exposure durations around 5 hours in air; strain rates in tensile tests of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative trade-off between the Al-induced oxide protection and any potential minor impacts on phase stability or ductility is not fully characterized.

paper_did: Prepared Nb‐24Ti‐18Si based alloys in three variants (ZX4, ZX6, ZX8) with a 5 at.% Sn addition (with additional Al and/or Cr) by arc melting, casting, and subsequent high‐temperature heat treatments.

Conducted detailed microstructural characterizations (using XRD, SEM coupled with EDS/EPMA) to identify phases (e.g., Nbss, βNb5Si3, αNb5Si3, Nb3Sn, and C14‐NbCr2 Laves phase) and to document macrosegregation phenomena.
Performed isothermal oxidation experiments in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 hours, recording weight gain kinetics and evaluating scale adhesion and spallation behavior.
Compared the oxidation behavior (e.g., pest suppression at 800 °C and scale spallation at 1200 °C) of the 5 at.% Sn alloys with analogous low‐Sn content alloys.
paper_reported: The 5 at.% Sn addition suppressed pest oxidation at 800 °C and promoted the formation of a continuous Sn‐rich area (containing compounds such as Nb3Sn, Nb5Sn2Si, and NbSn2) beneath the oxide scale.
Different alloys (ZX4, ZX6, ZX8) exhibited varying oxidation kinetics (parabolic and/or linear regimes) and microstructural evolutions, with ZX6 showing improved scale adhesion at 1200 °C.

Macrosegregation in the cast alloys influenced the distribution of key phases, and the stability of phases (e.g., complete transformation of primary βNb5Si3 to αNb5Si3) was observed following heat treatment.
The oxide scales formed at both temperatures comprised mixtures of Nb‐rich, Nb+Si‐rich, and other titanium‐rich oxides, with oxygen contamination occurring via the Nbss phase.
paper_proposed: Future investigations were suggested to optimize the Sn concentration and to clarify its role in suppressing pest oxidation, including the mechanism by which a Sn‐rich interfacial area enhances oxidation resistance.
Additional work was proposed to explore how the synergy between Sn and other alloying additions (such as Al and Cr) influences phase stability and scale adhesion.

The minor Al addition is expected to oxidize preferentially, forming a protective alumina layer that reduces oxygen ingress. This should mitigate the detrimental oxidation (pesting) observed in the unalloyed equiatomic base, while preserving the bulk mechanical properties due to low concentration.

paper_did: Developed and processed three refractory metal intermetallic composite/complex concentrated alloys (TT5, TT6, TT7) based on Nb with alloying additions of B plus either Ta, Sn, or Hf using arc‐melting and heat treatment at 1500 °C for 100 h.

Conducted comprehensive microstructural and phase identification studies using X‐RD and EPMA; measured density, macrosegregation of key solutes (B, Si, Ti), hardness (both bulk and micro‐hardness), and oxidation behavior (mass gain, scale spallation) at 800 and 1200 °C.
Applied the NICE (Niobium Intermetallic Composite Elaboration) alloy design methodology to correlate alloy/phase parameters (VEC, δ, Δχ, etc.) with the observed properties.

paper_did: Synthesized three refractory complex concentrated alloys (TT5, TT6, TT7) based on the Nb‐Ti‐Cr‐Al‐B‐Si system with one extra element (Ta in TT5, Sn in TT6, Hf in TT7) using arc melting and repeated remelting to form button ingots, followed by a 100‐h heat treatment at 1500 °C.

Characterized the alloys’ microstructures and phase compositions with XRD, EPMA, and SEM, identifying phases such as the bcc Nb solid solution (Nbss), T2 silicide, D88 silicide, and in one case Nb3Sn or Nb3Si.

Measured physical properties including density (all below 7 g/cm³), hardness (both bulk and microhardness of individual phases), and specific strength (notably, TT6 exhibited the highest specific strength), and analyzed macrosegregation of key solutes (B, Si, and Ti).
Tested isothermal oxidation behavior at 800 °C and 1200 °C for up to 100 hours, reporting on mass gain, scale spallation, and kinetics; and compared oxidation performance to B‐free reference alloys.
paper_reported: The addition of alloying elements (Hf, Sn, Ta) in B-containing RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs modifies macrosegregation—reducing segregation of B, Si, and Ti—and influences phase stability.

TT5 and TT7, with compositions including Si (around 18 at.%), showed stable bcc Nbss along with T2 and D88 silicides, while TT6 formed Nb3Sn along with T2 and D88 silicides; density values remained below 7 g/cm³ and TT6 had the highest specific strength even after heat treatment.

Oxidation experiments revealed that, at 800 °C none of the B-containing alloys suffered pest oxidation (although some scales spalled), while at 1200 °C scales on TT6 and TT7 remained adherent, with clear differences in oxidation kinetics among the alloys.
paper_proposed: Further research is needed to understand the detailed synergy between boron and the additional alloying elements (Sn, Hf, Ta) on solute macrosegregation and oxidation behavior.

The paper suggests that fine‐tuning the phase composition and microstructural homogeneity via the NICE alloy design methodology may lead to improved oxidation resistance and a better balance of high‐temperature properties.

Additional investigations might explore processing routes or compositional variations to further control phase stability, macrosegregation, and scale adherence under high‐temperature oxidative conditions.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A surface fluorination treatment on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will induce the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (dominated by HfO2 with contributions from other refractory oxides) that retards oxygen ingress at high temperatures.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting none or poorly protective native oxide scales with inadequate oxygen resistance.
hypotheses.intervention: Spray the alloy’s polished surface with a low‐concentration aqueous solution of NaF (or similar fluorine compound) prior to high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose treated specimens to air at ~1000 °C for 100 h (or similar durations relevant to high-temperature service) with uniaxial or negligible loading to simulate service conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A continuous oxide layer enriched in HfO2 (and possibly mixed with Nb/Ta oxides), whose formation is promoted by fluorine-induced volatilization and selective oxidation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Fluorine reacts at the metal surface to form transient metal‐fluorides (e.g. HfF4) that preferentially volatilize, thereby locally depleting reactive species and promoting the selective oxidation of Hf to form a dense, slowly growing HfO2 layer. This continuous oxide acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion, analogous to the Al2O3 scale seen in fluorine-treated Ti–Al–Nb alloys (PMC9030595, sections 1–4).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will show greatly reduced oxidation weight gain (on the order of a 70–80% reduction relative to untreated material, based on analogous behavior in TiAl systems) and improved scale adhesion, while retaining its useful room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits rapid oxidation and deleterious oxide scale exfoliation at 1000 °C.
hypotheses.boundary: Test validity is confined to high-temperature static air exposure (~1000 °C, up to 100 h) without significant mechanical load; tensile properties are measured at room and service temperatures to confirm no significant degradation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement and the dominant oxide phase in the fluorine-treated HfNbTaTiZr may differ from the TiAl system; the 70–80% improvement is estimated from a similar mechanistic process but remains uncertain.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: An ultrathin, continuous oxide scale (likely dominated by HfO2 with possible contributions from Nb/Ta oxides) that forms coherently and acts as a barrier against oxygen diffusion.
hypotheses.mechanism: The low oxygen partial pressure during pre-oxidation facilitates the controlled formation of a uniform and adherent oxide layer that 'seeds' a stable barrier. hypotheses.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature service in air around 1000 °C for extended exposures (up to 100 h) and under conditions where the pre-oxidation does not alter the bulk microstructure.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact composition and protective nature of the pre-formed oxide, as well as quantitative improvements in oxidation resistance, are not well established but are expected to be positive based on analogous pre-oxidation treatments in other alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor alloying addition of aluminum (around 2–5 at.% Al substitution) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can improve its oxygen resistance while preserving its mechanical performance by enabling the formation of a continuous, slow-growing protective Al2O3 scale at high temperature.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a BCC-dominated microstructure that currently exhibits poor oxygen resistance at high temperatures.
hypotheses.intervention: Substitute a small fraction (2–5 at.%) of one of the base elements (for example, partially replacing Ti) with Al during alloy synthesis.
hypotheses.conditions: Oxidation exposure in air at 800–1000 °C for durations up to 100 h; mechanical testing at room temperature and high temperature (around 1000 °C) under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale on the surface that adheres to the substrate with minimal spallation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong tendency to form stable, dense Al2O3 due to its low Gibbs free energy of oxide formation. Adding Al enables a rapid formation of an adherent oxide layer which minimizes oxygen diffusion into the substrate. By keeping the Al content low, the bulk phase and its mechanical properties are retained, while the surface exhibits enhanced oxidation resistance similar to the behavior seen in AlCoCrFeNi coatings where selective oxidation of Al occurred.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Enhanced oxidation resistance (reduced mass gain and oxide scale thickness) compared to the untreated alloy, with little to no degradation in room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (~163–530 MPa).
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that suffers from rapid oxygen penetration and scale growth resulting in poor oxidation resistance at high temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: Temperatures: 800–1000 °C; Atmosphere: Air; Exposure time: up to 100 h; Mechanical loading: Tensile loading as per standard test strain rates.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact balance between improving oxidation resistance and preserving the original phase stability and ductility may require optimization; precise quantitative improvement is to be determined.

paper_did: Prepared AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy coatings by atmospheric plasma spraying using commercial gas‐atomized powders on Ni‐based substrates.
Subjected the coatings to isothermal oxidation in air at temperatures from 650 °C to 1000 °C for various durations (20 h, 50 h, 100 h, and even 200 h in some cases).

Characterized the coatings using X‐ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and elemental mapping to track phase transitions and oxide scale formation.
paper_reported: At the initial stage of oxidation a mixed, laminated oxide scale formed on the coating surface, which evolved into a continuous, alumina‐rich (Al2O3) scale at higher temperatures (800–1000 °C).

Internal diffusion of aluminum led to an aluminum‐poor zone beneath the oxide layer and was accompanied by a BCC/B2 to FCC transition in the coating interior; in parallel, distinct Fe–Cr rich disordered (A2) and Al–Ni rich ordered (B2) phases emerged.

The study clarified that selective oxidation of Al (due to its low Gibbs free energy of oxide formation) controlled the oxide scale composition and that phase transformations were closely linked to elemental redistribution during oxidation.
paper_proposed: The paper underscores the need for further investigation into the oxidation mechanism of high-entropy coatings, particularly the role of elemental diffusion and phase transformation during high-temperature exposure.

It implies that understanding and controlling selective oxidation (e.g., promoting continuous Al2O3 layer formation) could be key for enhancing oxidation resistance, suggesting future work on the relationship between alloy composition, processing conditions, and resultant oxide scale structure.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, dense alumina coating on the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy using bias‐assisted HiPIMS will improve its oxygen resistance by providing an external diffusion barrier, while maintaining its inherent mechanical properties.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
hypotheses.intervention: Deposit a ~2–5 μm thick alumina (Al2O3) top layer on the alloy surface via a bias‐assisted high‐power impulse magnetron sputtering (HiPIMS) process.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposure to air at temperatures up to 800 °C for at least 5 h at strain rates of 10^–4–10^–2 s^–1; experiments on both uncoated and coated samples for direct comparison.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A dense, low-porosity Al2O3 scale with minimal columnar defects and strong adhesion to the substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: The densified alumina layer, produced under additional negative substrate bias (which enhances film density as seen in the multilayer CrAlN/Al2O3 coatings [PMC10806925::web::008]), limits oxygen ingress. Alumina is thermodynamically stable and forms a slow-growing, protective scale that prevents rapid oxidation of the underlying alloy without significantly altering its bulk mechanical performance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A marked reduction in oxygen uptake and pesting during high-temperature exposure (≥800 °C) relative to untreated material, with preserved room- and high-temperature strength and ductility. The improvement should be qualitatively higher than in uncoated cast alloy, though precise quantification is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from excessive oxidation (oxygen resistance issues) under the same conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: Valid for exposures in air from room temperature up to 800 °C, with exposure times on the order of hours (≥5 h); mechanical loading must not damage the thin coating.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact thickness and deposition parameters needed to match adhesion and uniformity requirements may vary; the quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is not precisely predictable without experimentation.

paper_did: Deposited a multilayer solar selective absorber stack using a combination of HiPIMS, RF, and DC magnetron sputtering, including a CrAlN multilayer with graded aluminum content followed by a top alumina (Al2O3) layer.
Applied a simultaneous DC‐pulsed negative bias (−100 V) during deposition on different substrates (SS316, Inconel 625, and silicon) to enhance film densification.

Subjected the coatings to short (2 h) and long (200 h) isothermal annealing treatments in air at temperatures of 600, 700, and 800 °C, and characterized their optical (solar absorptance, thermal emittance) and structural (XRD, SEM, TEM/EDX, Raman) properties.
paper_reported: That bias‐assisted deposition produced a denser, less columnar microstructure which improved thermal stability and oxidation resistance of the multilayer stack compared to coatings deposited without bias.

High solar absorptance (~94–95%) and low thermal emittance (~15–18%) were maintained even after annealing at elevated temperatures, with the onset of degradation (e.g. Cr2N formation) delayed relative to unbiased coatings.
